title: The date-sort error handler is itself broken, so a bad orderedDate loses the hearing

oracle.activityBoundary: every callActivity argument and return value crosses oracle/lib/boundary.js
oracle.determinismCheck: the case was run twice at clockPinIso and the two document arrays compared

swallowedErrors: [Hearing ID: 1828f356-f746-4f2d-932b-79ef2df95c80] - Exception in SetInformantRegister TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'log')

edits: hearing: each TFL defendant's offences[0].judicialResults truncated to its FIRST element, so every defendant context holds exactly one result and the per-defendant sort at DefendantContextBaseService.js:296 never calls its comparator.

hearing: prosecutionCases[0].defendants[1].offences[0].judicialResults[0].orderedDate set to "not/a/date". The other stays "2020-01-20", so the Set handed to RegisterFragmentService.getLatestOrderedDate holds two distinct values and Array#sort must call ITS comparator.

digests.convention: sha256 of the written file bytes — `sha256sum <file>` reproduces each value exactly

nodeEvidence.what: `const getLatestOrderedDate = (datesToSort) => { try { [...datesToSort].sort((a,b) => dateService.parse(b).getTime() - dateService.parse(a).getTime()) ...` — a module-scope ARROW function, so `this` is the module scope, not an object with a context.

parse(dateString, format = 'YYYY/MM/DD') throws `new Error('Invalid date format')` when moment cannot parse. Note the default format is slash-separated while the fixture data is hyphen-separated ISO; moment's non-strict parsing tolerates the mismatch, which is why this has never been noticed.

`catch (ex) { //TODO HOW THE ORCHESTRATOR WILL HANDLE THIS.  this.context.log(...) }` — `this.context` is undefined here, so the catch block throws TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'log'). The error handler destroys the error.
getLatestOrderedDate is called at :74, outside any inner try, so the TypeError escapes to the activity catch at :159 and the hearing is lost.

assertion: Each of the two TFL defendants is reduced to exactly ONE judicial result, and the second defendant's orderedDate is "not/a/date". Both details are load-bearing and neither may be "simplified": one result per defendant keeps DefendantContextBaseService.getLatestOrderedDate (which sorts PER DEFENDANT and would otherwise throw first — see s06-unguarded-date-parse-in-defendant-context) below the two-element threshold at which Array#sort invokes a comparator, while the two DISTINCT dates across defendants push RegisterFragmentService.getLatestOrderedDate above it. Assert EXACTLY: (1) expected.json is JSON null; (2) meta.json observed.outcome is "swallowed-exception"; (3) observed.swallowedErrors has exactly one entry, from SetInformantRegister, and it is a TypeError whose message names 'log' — NOT the Error("Invalid date format") that was actually raised. Assert on the TypeError specifically. It is the fingerprint of the broken catch block: the error handler destroyed the diagnosis before anyone could read it, and the operator is left with a hearing that vanished and a message about a missing property. Parity requirement: zero documents. The Java port MUST NOT sort defensively past a bad date and MUST NOT pick the parseable date and carry on — either would be an unregistered fix. It MUST, unlike Node, classify and persist the failure. If a future reader is tempted to make the Java sort null-safe "because it is obviously a bug": it is, and fixing it is welcome, in a commit that also adds the DEVIATIONS.md row and updates this expectation.
